title: Cuthbert and the otters
hook: after praying all night in the sea, Cuthbert is warmed by otters

segments.voice: Yesterday, Caedmon's song, the shy cowherd who sang of creation. Your line was even the shy sing. Where did you hum? Day seven hundred ninety-three.

Somebody is following him. It's the middle of the night at a monastery by the sea, and a guest, a monk named Cuthbert, has slipped out while everyone sleeps. He does this, apparently. One of the brothers has noticed, and tonight curiosity wins. He creeps out after him, keeping his distance, down toward the shore. He expects, maybe, to catch the holy man doing something ordinary. Instead he watches Cuthbert walk straight into the sea, deeper and deeper, until the cold water is up around his neck. And there he stays. Today, what the brother saw, and what he did after.
screen: `INTO THE SEA, UP TO HIS NECK.`

segments.voice: The story comes from Bede, who wrote a life of Cuthbert. Cuthbert stands in the sea through the dark hours, Bede says, singing praises to God with the waves. When dawn comes he wades out and kneels on the sand to pray. And then two small animals come up out of the sea after him. They stretch out in front of him, warm his feet with their breath, and dry them with their fur. When they're done, Cuthbert blesses them, and they slip back into the water. The story is known today as Cuthbert and the otters. Then there's the brother watching from the shore. Bede says he's so shaken by what he's seen that he can barely walk home. In the morning he goes to Cuthbert and falls at his feet, in tears, asking forgiveness for spying. Cuthbert knows already. And he's gentle. He forgives him, on one condition: tell no one what you saw while I'm alive. The brother keeps the promise, and only after Cuthbert's death does the story come out. So there are two kindnesses in it. Animals caring for a man who was cold, and a man caring for a brother who was ashamed. Cuthbert later lived on Lindisfarne, the island Aidan came to from Iona a few days back in our story. Some readers see in the otters creation at peace with a holy person, like Adam among the animals in Eden. Others keep it simply as a story of two kindnesses on one cold shore.

Here's the practice: notice an animal's kindness. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind an animal that has been gentle with you or with someone you love. A dog that leans against your leg on a bad day. A cat that sits on the one person who's sad. A bird at the window. Even an animal you only watched once, caring for its young. Stay with that picture. Notice how it was given without words, and without asking anything back. If you pray, you can give thanks for it. If you don't, just let yourself be warmed by the memory. The bell holds the time.
Cuthbert. A monk who stood in prayer in the cold sea at night, and whose feet two otters warmed at dawn, in a secret kept until he died.
Your line: the sea and the otters. Today, be warm to someone who's been out in the cold, and if you see a kindness, let it be theirs to tell. Day seven hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Christians in the north of England and the Scottish borders honor Saint Cuthbert, and pilgrims visit Lindisfarne, where he lived, and Durham Cathedral, where tradition places his shrine.

notes: Bede, prose Life of Cuthbert 10 (the visit to Abbess Ebbe at Coldingham): sea up to the neck (some versions: arms), praise through the night, kneeling on the shore, two sea animals warm and dry his feet, blessing, the brother's fear, forgiveness, secrecy until Cuthbert's death. Paraphrased; confirm. The anonymous Life tells the same story.
Whether Bede names the animals as otters ('lutraeae') or only as sea creatures: confirm. The script says only that the story is known today as 'Cuthbert and the otters'.
'Cuthbert later lived on Lindisfarne': prior and later bishop there, and hermit on Inner Farne; confirm phrasing.
The two readings (creation at peace with the holy; a gentle story) are offered without ranking; confirm.
'Cuthbert knows already': Bede has Cuthbert respond as one who already knew what the brother had done; confirm.
howItsDone: Durham as the place of his shrine is attributed to tradition; confirm.
Editor: cut the stock 'the part people tend to forget'; 'spends the night afraid' replaced with Bede's 'can barely walk home'.

Audit: myth reveal no longer claims Cuthbert 'didn't know anyone was watching' (Bede has him already know by morning); the closing readings no longer assert 'the way things were meant to be' in the narrator's voice, and the Eden reading is given to 'some readers'.
